item.text: {"text":"Closest match: [UFRec (May 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.28493), combining next-item prediction with parallel multi-step future supervision and contrastive alignment to pooled future-item embeddings. Auxiliary supervision receives less weight when next-item prediction entropy is high; both auxiliary modules disappear at inference. This directly supports changing representation learning without changing deployed scoring. Earlier evidence includes a [2023 Edinburgh thesis](https://project-archive.inf.ed.ac.uk/msc/20236290/msc_proj.pdf) combining next-item and all-action prediction, reporting improvements on MovieLens-1M with sampled-softmax training. Its backbone is SASRec, so these results do not establish gains for GRU4Rec. The foundational [PinnerFormer (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04507) similarly learns persistent preferences through dense supervision from longer-term future actions.\n\nFor the constrained GRU experiment, a plausible adaptation is one causal GRU trained with its ordinary next-item loss plus low-weight horizon-specific projections predicting items two to several steps ahead. Optionally align a projection of the same recurrent state with pooled future-item embeddings. This is an inferred design, not a demonstrated GRU result from these sources. Keep every auxiliary target inside the training history, mask unavailable horizons, and feed only the prefix into the GRU. Retain one next-item scoring head and one checkpoint per category at inference, reading the final nonpadding position. Compare against next-item-only training using the fixed macro validation HR@10: longer-horizon supervision may improve persistent preference learning, but excessive weight can dilute immediate next-item accuracy."}
